query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding reactive elements like Y or Ce to refractory high-entropy alloys will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a protective oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys in their as-cast state
generation.intervention: Adding 1 at.% of Y or Ce to the alloy composition
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 1000°C for 100 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous and dense oxide layer rich in Y or Ce
generation.mechanism: The added Y or Ce reacts with oxygen to form a stable oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation of the alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxidation rate by at least 50% compared to the untreated alloy
generation.boundary: Oxidation rate measured by weight gain per unit area
generation.uncertainty: The actual oxidation rate reduction may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the oxidation rates of refractory high-entropy alloys with and without Y or Ce additions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation rate of the alloy with Y or Ce additions is not significantly lower than that of the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)”, has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases. Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al. as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported. However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. For high temperature applications, formation of Al2O3, Cr2O3, or SiO2 layer can provide oxidation resistance since these oxides are thermodynamically stable and exhibit low oxygen permeability. Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
